Hey, this thread may be for Fixer's fans, but his critics are allowed. We just all have to know that we can't convince each other - and maybe try to give hints or advices on the way to play him.

About Wraith and Fixer : I think the main difference between the two is that Wraith cards and combos have a big "Wow!" factor. She has a lot of possible combos, and a lot of cards that seem/are obviously good. While Fixer can do many of the things our beloved mummy in a swimming suit does, but with cards that look meh.

The way we look at heroes (and at villains, even) depends a lot on how "amazing" they feel when we play them - especially the first times we play them. Expatriette's shotgun may be the best one-target damage power around, it feels less awesome than Ra's base power of burning people alive. Playing Wraith feels like opening a toy chest full of marvels - while Fixer's feel like opening a greasy toolbox.

My own experience is that, after playing a lot all heroes, they all have roughly the same "problem" : sometimes, you can't do anything interesting with them, because they don't have the cards they need. Even with a lot of drawing, you often can't manage to do much. It is true of Mr Fixer, it is also true of Wraith - I have had games were she was a dead weight, unable to do anything valuable for 3 rounds in a row but hide herself. It happens to everyone.

There's another thing to take into account : the BIG difference beween playing solo or with other players. Maybe it explains, at least in part, why heroes like Expatriette, Mr Fixer, Absolute Zeo or Bunker are seen as sub-par. When I play solo, I play the team as a whole - one of the heroes may have a bad turn, I don't really care, I have 3 other heroes to have fun with. In a multiplayer game, it can feel very different - spending a few rounds doing nothing big while the other players seem to chain amazing moves can be unpleasant, both for the player and his team mates…

I think that is the problem with some heroes of the base game and rook city : though they are as capable as their colleagues, they may not be as "shiny" to play than the others, at least at first. I think we won't see this with future heroes - this is the kind of problem the play testers help to mitigate.

As for why Wraith is in the "lower end" of the scale according to the survey… I am not sure. Maybe because she has a harder time to get her combos out than you might think at first glance - she has a long setup time when/if you don't have Impromptu Invention in hand. Maybe because she has many different "roles" she can perform - but only a few of them are really useful in a given fight. There are times when Infrared Goggles, for instance, are less useful than damage, or tanking/stunning. And vice versa. I know that I sometime chose the wrong tactics - or can't manage to have the cards I would need… Her deck feels awesome - and in fact IS awesome - but you rarely can use it all in a given game.

By the way - I will here give my only negative "critic" to flamethrower49's marvelous guides : they are very useful and enlightening, but they give the feeling that it is "normal" to have all these beautiful combos and cards. It is what I call "the Argent Adept fallacy" : yes, you can, sometimes, have AA use all his instruments in a given turn. it happens, I've seen it. But in most of my games, he can't manage to have more than a few cards and an instrument in play - most games are played too fast for a big set up. He can be quite effective even with only one or two cards, and I like him. But his big setup is as rare as Bunker's or AZ's, or Nightmist's. Most of the time, heroes have to improvize with what they have, and what they have is not shiny at all. I think we may need some kind of "improvizing with your hand" guide someday ! (Flamethrower49, I like your guides ! They are great ! Don't take this "critic" negatively ! Biggest Fan ! )

This!  This!  Forever this!

My Friday night group played again over the weekend in lieu of our normal Hell on Earth game, and one of our newest players took Bunker for the evening.  He's an old school Magic player, and a little bit of a min-maxer–then again, that's the pot calling the kettle black, there–but I just could not for the life of me figure out what he was doing all game.  

Bunker may well be my favorite character in the set, simply because I'm a giant Iron Man fanboy.  I've played him probably more than any other character.  So, when I saw Dan spending turn after turn just collecting cards and not dealing damage, I felt like I wanted to scream at him, "Dude!  You're doing it wrong!"  Countless times, when buffed and with Grenade Launcher in hand, he chose to forgo mowing down minions in favor of simply drawing more cards.  His justification was that he was building a big enough deck to power the OmniCannon and the Gatling Gun simultaneously.  Meanwhile, we kept getting hammered by foes and, expectedly, his exasperation when we'd hit equipment-destroying cards was almost tearful, after he'd spent turn after turn building up with little actual effect on the game.

I find that as I play more and more–particularly as I've tried playing solo, which has helped me understand a lot more of the complex cards in the deck–the allure of the Big Damn Combo becomes less and less.  It's awesome when it happens, but the likelihood of a huge, 30-40 damage turn just isn't likely.  I'd rather be able to put out 6-10 damage on a regular basis, while slowly expanding an arsenal of tricks, rather than bank multiple turns on a plan that could be nullified by the flip of a single card.  Given the example above?  I find that I very rarely try to do both the Gatling Gun and the OmniCannon–between card discards and rebuffs nuking my Ammo Drops, I find that I never have enough cards to run both effectively.  But, by committing to one, coupled with the Flak Cannon or Grenade Launcher, I can put out consistent, potent damage while keeping my hand full of options for deck control and recovery.  

I guess what I like about Fixer, then, is his zen-like simplicity.  He doesn't need a specific tool or a specific style to contribute–he just needs A style or tool.  And, once he has that, his cards become a pool of options rather than necessary plays.  Damage reduction?  He's got a style for that.  Lots of dudes?  Jackhandle has it covered.  And, when he's got the right option in play, he can lay down Overdrive or Bloody Knuckles for added damage.  The key is to simply flow with the situation, and not get attached to finding the "perfect dream combo".

I don't want to put words in SoundofTrees' mouth, so take anything I say with a grain of salt, brother.

 

Imagine if you will, a 500 piece jigsaw puzzle in a blank cardboard box.  As you open the box, you have no idea what the overall picture is supposed to be and how the pieces will fit together.  After an hour or so of fitting pieces together, you begin to see a patterns emerge.  You might start at the edge and build a framework, allowing you to access deeper and deeper within the puzzle itself.  Eventually, the more time you devote to it, the closer you get to understanding the whole picture, even without seeing the original image.

Now, imagine doing the same puzzle while looking at the box lid with a picture on the cover.  If it's an image of a carnival, you might start right in the middle of the puzzle, looking for bits of the Ferris Wheel in the middle of the puzzle, rather than at the edge.  While the reference image simultaneously makes your life easier by giving you a point of reference and an overall sense of direction, it also builds in the inborn temptation to skew away from the "basic" framework of the puzzle.

 

Your guides are great, brother.  After I picked up Sentinels a few weeks ago, they really helped me to understand how the heroes function, what roles they fill within a given group, and what cards to keep an eye on.  But, when you know what the "ideal" hero set-up is supposed to be, can anyone resist the temptation to try to fulfill that vision?  And, in trying to fulfill that 'ultimate combo', it can become easy to lose sight of the actual goal of defeating the villain–I saw that problem firsthand with Dan, in the example I had earlier.  He was more focused on getting that Gatling/OmniCannon/FlakCannon combo rolling, rather than actually winning the game as the group.

I'm not trying to say that your guides are "cheating" or that someone should have to "make their bones" by playing the game raw first–rather, it's just tempting to see the potential in an "ideal scenario" and hold an unspoken expectation that "Hey, this guy can do X, Y, and Z.  I should be able to do that!"

Case in point?  I've never managed to get the Wrest the Mind / Telekinetic Cocoon combo to work.  I see the obvious appeal–redirect damage away from allies, while damaging enemies?  Awesome idea!–but each time the possibility has come up, I've found myself needing to use a Power or play a different card, or something simply makes the combo untenable.  But, the temptation for me is still there, each time I play Visionary:  can I pull off this combo?  Can I drop the big damage with Bunker or Absolute Zero?  

Robert Penn Warren wrote in "All the King's Men" that "The end of man is to know."  Man's demise would come either from the knowledge he hasn't got (being a rookie, playing a game the first time) or the knowledge that he has got (knowing how cards are played and trying to subconsciously go for the 'high score' rather than winning the game).  Even as our overt, stated goal would be to win the game cooperatively, there's still a niggling temptation "down in the dark, which is you" that wants to achieve the 'impossible'.

For what it's worth?  I still like your guides and I still want to see more of them.  I really hope you finish out the remaining set, particularly as Shattered Timelines comes out.  I just have to keep them in perspective in terms of my own play, and find what works best for me.  And, y'know…more perspectives are always good!

I'll try to be clearer - and keep in mind that it is very subjective. When someone asks, on these forums, how to fight a given villain, or better use an environment, or which hero can be the more useful in a given situation, the answers often are very specific. For instance, Haka is often cited as a good hero to have against the Matriarch, because of Savage Mana. But Savage Mana is just one card in his deck, that you may never see in a given fight. We are often fascinated by great combos, or perfect card uses. And when we read guides or hints/advices, we tend to remember the most the awesome combos (or the things we never thought of before). This is not a problem with your guides, but with our attitude : we tend, when asked how to play a hero, to first think of the times something big happened, when the other player's jaws dropped on the floor. We often forget the other times, when our beloved hero did nothing special… The anecdote becomes the focus of our thought on this hero/villain, etc.

I tend to "defend" Mr Fixer (or Expatriette) because I've seen him "rock the casbah" on multiple occassion - even if I've seen him spend other games doing nothing much. On the other hand, I first didn't like the Argent Adept : I had read so much about him being awesome that the first times I played him, I was unimpressed, as he did not manage to put big combos out. I'm just beginning to like him, but not because of the big card combos, because of the little things he can do that seem less awesome than the "play every power" trick but are so damn useful.

I should not have associated this with your guides - I'll confess I maybe failed to prevent myself from trying to be provocative. This is more about our attitude, has a forum crowd of SotM fans. We are fond of the awesomeness that happens in this game, and often forget the less awesome games where our heroes do nothing "big", the villain keeps being un-impressive, and nothing memorable happens.

We build expectations about what heroes should do, how difficul villains should be - and are disappointed when these expectations are not met. But our expectations are often built on very "perfect" anecdotes, leading to bigger disappointment, and, often preventing us to be imaginative and improvize with what we have, because it feels "subpar".

Bunker and AZ, for instance, fall easily into this "trap" : as pointed in the guide for Bunker, Mode cards are not the center of his deck, but useful tools that you will only use some times - but many players, at first, try to use them at all cost (I did…) Likewise, AZ can play a whole game without ever using his modules and still be effective - but it feels "wrong" to play like this if you don't know him well. TheSoundOfTrees:

I think the problem many players have with Mr F is that his role in the team is not obvious. He seems to be a damage dealer, at first glance, but in fact is not. His main job is to let other heroes fight at maximum efficiency by disposing of damage reduction, either by killing "guards" or bypassing other damage reduction cards.

Absolutely.  After about my second game with him I realized he is a primarily tank that can help keep small targets off the board.  That is how I have played him ever since and he has seemed much more capable.  If I can find a mantis stance early I'm set, throw in a tool and its go time.  Just fine since my group loves tanks anyway.
